latin.360: PLAC. Cum Calvinus opponit naturam judicio Dei in hoc negotio, non id facit, ut neget naturali propagatione ab Adamo in posteros manasse corruptionem, nec per judicium Dei intelligit judiciariam imputationem peccati actualis Adami, aut poenae inflictionem. Dicimus, inquit, naturali hominem vitiositate corruptum, sed quae a natura non fluxerit. A natura fluxisse negamus, ut significemus adventitiam magis esse qualitatem, quae homini acciderit, quam substantialem proprietatem quae ab initio indita fuerit. Per judicium, aut potius consilium, Dei intelligit illud, quo Deus permisit & praeordinavit ut lapsum Adami, sic lapsus propagationem; id quod a nobis cap. XIII. huius Manuscripti fusius demonstratum est, nec uspiam refutatur a viro docto.
latin.361: GAR. An vero, cum Deus corruptionem personalem omnium hominum non permittat in posteros descendere, corruptionem, inquam, non nativam ex Adamo naturaliter omnibus insitam, sed ascititiam, & ex actualibus peccatis progerminantem, putandus est contra naturae ordinem agere, aut leges naturalis propagationis evertere, aut peccati actualis naturalem sequelam impedire? Vix dictum putem hactenus a quoquam, aut cogitatum.
latin.362: PLAC. Iam ostendi, valde disparem esse rationem primi peccati actualis, & sequentium; illud corrupisse naturam, ista non item; necnon corruptionis universalis in aversione a vero fine ultimo & conversione ad finem ultimum falso apparentem sitae, & corruptionis illius particularis determinationis ad certa quaedam objecta; illam enim naturaliter propagari, hanc non item; illam non nisi per regenerationem tolli posse, hanc posse nonnunquam absque regeneratione aut tolli, aut etiam in oppositam mutari. Non igitur virum doctum supponere decuit, eandem esse utriusque rationem.
latin.363: GAR. Denique de actu generationis quod additur, in quo homines peccant, & Deum offendunt, & merito a Deo deseruntur, ad rem praesentem parum facere videtur: quandoquidem hic non de justo judicio Dei erga generantes, sed erga genitos agitur: aut si justum illud judicium respicere dicatur filios, qui corrupti merito nascantur, quia genitores in actu generationis peccarunt & Deum offenderunt: quis non videt inde nobis emergere conclusionem, cui tam infestus est Vir doctus, peccati paterni poenas in filios descendere?
latin.364: PLAC. De peccati patris imputatione non ad causam quam agit vir doctus, sed ad meam, qui reddere rationem volui, cur Deus propagationem peccati permiserit. Non modo enim non tenebatur impedire naturae cursum, sed ne impediret, obstabant constitutae ante lapsum leges, & ipsa generantium peccata desertionem promerentia. Hoc autem consilium seu judicium, cum spectet ad generantes eatenus sua naturae permittendos, aliquomodo ad genitos spectare dici potest: nec tamen propterea est judicium, quo generantis peccatum imputatur generando. Nam aliud est decretum de non impediendo peccato, aut peccati contagio seu dimanatione a parente in liberos, aliud decretum de irroganda secundum legis comminationem poena.
latin.365: Hoc supponit existentiam & peccatum illius qui punitur. Imputare enim peccatum nondum existenti, punire nondum existentem, mihi paradoxum videtur.

pass_a.360: Placeus reads Calvin's nature-versus-judgment opposition as not denying that corruption passed by natural propagation from Adam, and not taking 'judgment' as forensic imputation of Adam's actual sin or infliction of punishment. Calvin's 'natural viciousness' is adventitious, not a substantial property from the start. By judgment—or rather counsel—he means God's permitting and preordaining both the fall and its propagation, as Placeus showed in Manuscript cap. XIII and GAR nowhere refutes.
pass_a.361: GAR asks: when God does not let each man's personal, adventitious corruption from his own actual sins descend to posterity—unlike the native Adamic corruption—is that acting against nature's order, overturning propagation laws, or blocking actual sin's natural sequel? He doubts anyone has said or even thought so.
pass_a.362: Placeus repeats the disparity: the first actual sin corrupted nature; later sins do not likewise. Universal corruption (aversion from the true last end / conversion to a false one) propagates naturally and yields only to regeneration; particular determinations to certain objects do not so propagate and can sometimes change without regeneration. GAR should not have supposed both share one reason.
pass_a.363: GAR says the generation-act point—parents sin, offend God, deserve desertion—does little here, because the present question is just judgment toward the begotten, not the begetters. If that judgment is said to hit sons born corrupt because parents sinned in generating, then the hated conclusion emerges: penalties of the father's sin descend on the sons.
pass_a.364: Placeus: talk of imputing the father's sin belongs to his own cause—why God permitted sin's propagation—not GAR's. God was not bound to stop nature's course; pre-fall laws and begetters' desertion-earning sins blocked hindrance. Counsel/judgment toward permitting begetters their nature can somehow regard the begotten, yet is not imputation of the begetter's sin to the child. Decree not to hinder contagion ≠ decree to inflict threatened punishment.
pass_a.365: The punishing decree presupposes the existence and sin of the one punished. To impute sin to one not yet existing, or punish one not yet existing, Placeus calls a paradox. Tip before Cap. VII on the three similitudes.

360: PLAC. When Calvin opposes nature to God's judgment in this business, he does not do it so as to deny that corruption flowed by natural propagation from Adam into posterity, nor by God's judgment does he understand a forensic imputation of Adam's actual sin, or an infliction of punishment. We say, he says, that man is corrupted by a natural viciousness, but one which did not flow from nature. That it flowed from nature we deny, to signify that it is rather an adventitious quality which befell man than a substantial property implanted from the beginning. By judgment, or rather counsel, of God he understands that by which God permitted and preordained both Adam's fall and the propagation of the fall—which we demonstrated more fully in cap. XIII of this Manuscript, and which is nowhere refuted by the learned man.
361: GAR. But when God does not permit the personal corruption of all men to descend into posterity—corruption, I say, not native and naturally implanted in all from Adam, but adventitious and sprouting from actual sins—is he to be thought to act against the order of nature, or to overturn the laws of natural propagation, or to hinder the natural sequel of actual sin? I can scarcely think this has hitherto been said by anyone, or even thought.
362: PLAC. I have already shown that the reason of the first actual sin and of those that follow is very unequal: that corrupted nature, these do not likewise; and also of universal corruption seated in aversion from the true last end and conversion to a falsely apparent last end, and of that particular determination of corruption to certain objects—for the former is naturally propagated, the latter not likewise; the former can be taken away only by regeneration, the latter can sometimes without regeneration be taken away or even changed into its opposite. Therefore the learned man ought not to have supposed that the reason of both is the same.
363: GAR. Finally, what is added about the act of generation, in which men sin and offend God and are deservedly deserted by God, seems to do little for the present matter: seeing that here it is not a question of God's just judgment toward begetters, but toward the begotten; or if that just judgment be said to regard sons who are deservedly born corrupt because parents in the act of generation sinned and offended God—who does not see that from there emerges for us the conclusion to which the learned man is so hostile, that the penalties of the father's sin descend upon the sons?
364: PLAC. Of the imputation of the father's sin—not to the cause the learned man is driving, but to mine, who wished to give a reason why God permitted the propagation of sin. For not only was he not bound to hinder nature's course, but that he might not hinder it, laws constituted before the fall stood in the way, and the very sins of begetters deserving desertion. But this counsel or judgment, since it regards begetters insofar as they are to be permitted their nature, can somehow be said to regard the begotten: yet it is not therefore a judgment by which the begetter's sin is imputed to the one being begotten. For one thing is a decree of not hindering sin, or the contagion or outflow of sin from parent into children; another is a decree of inflicting punishment according to the law's threat.
365: This latter presupposes the existence and the sin of him who is punished. For to impute sin to one not yet existing, to punish one not yet existing, seems to me a paradox.
